articles.author: Enes
articles.description:
Introduction: Why Another Nearby Discovery App?


Traditional social networks are optimized for permanent connections and algorithmic feeds, while modern dating apps rely heavily on endless swipe decks. When you travel to a new city, work out of a local cafe, or attend a tech conference, you often don't want a heavy social network—you just want to know who is nearby, what vibe they share, and have a zero-friction way to break the ice.
This was the motivation behind SayHi: Wave Nearby, a native iOS application built entirely in Swift and SwiftUI.
Using MapKit's latest SwiftUI declarative Map APIs in iOS 17 and iOS 18:
Clustered Annotations: Dynamic annotation clustering ensures that in dense urban areas, rendering 100+ avatar pins does not trigger main-thread hitches.
Dynamic Camera Framing: Seamless camera easing between localized neighborhood zoom and regional discovery.
User privacy is paramount when building location-aware software:
No Precise GPS Over The Wire: Exact latitude and longitude coordinates are never stored or broadcast.
Sector Randomization: Coordinates are quantized and fuzzed into randomized grid sectors (~200m radius), computing approximate proximity without revealing exact buildings or residences.
Instead of cold messaging or forced matching:
Users tap to send a Wave!
A wave triggers a fluid, hardware-accelerated spring animation using SwiftUI's PhaseAnimator.
When both users wave at each other, an ephemeral chat opens up.
Users can toggle explicit intentions in real time:
Grab Coffee
Explore the City
Workout / Gym Partner
Casual Conversation
SayHi is currently live worldwide on the App Store:
Download on App Store: SayHi: Wave Nearby


Tech Stack: 100% Swift, SwiftUI, MapKit, CoreLocation, Combine/Async-Await.
Would love to hear feedback from the developer community on location clustering, privacy design, and SwiftUI ergonomics!
articles.title: Building SayHi: An Ephemeral Proximity Discovery iOS App with SwiftUI & MapKit

articles.author: Nick Fasulo
articles.description:
I recently added a chatbot feature to Galaxy Movies, my movie discovery app.
The idea came from a problem I run into all the time: there are too many movies to choose from, and browsing doesn’t always help.
You can scroll through trending lists, genres, ratings, and streaming options, but sometimes what you really want is to ask a simple question: “What should I watch tonight?”
So I built Galaxy Bot.
Galaxy Bot is a conversational movie assistant that helps users find movies based on what they actually want in the moment. Instead of only relying on filters, users can describe their mood, who they’re watching with, how much time they have, or what kind of movie they’re trying to avoid.
Some example prompts:
“Recommend a feel-good movie under two hours.”
“I want a sci-fi movie that isn’t too confusing.”
“What should I watch with my family?”
“Give me something tense but not horror.”
The main thing I focused on was making the chatbot feel useful without getting in the way. It should make discovery faster, not make the app feel heavier.
This first version is about helping users get unstuck when they don’t know what to watch. Over time, I’d like to make it better at understanding taste, saved movies, ratings, and streaming availability.
You can check it out here: Galaxy Movies
articles.title: I Added a Chatbot to My Movie Discovery App

articles.description:
Most APIs were designed for two consumers: a human reading documentation and code a human wrote once. An AI agent is neither. It discovers endpoints at runtime from a machine-readable description, fills in arguments by pattern-matching field names, retries automatically when something fails, and chains five calls together without anyone watching each step. APIs that are merely usable by humans are frequently misusable by agents, and the misuse looks like success until it creates a duplicate charge or a deleted record.
The good news: the properties that make an API agent-friendly are the same mature API design practices that help human integrators. This article covers the six that matter most, with concrete request and response shapes.
An agent will retry your call. It will retry because a …
articles.title: Designing APIs for AI Agents: Idempotency, Machine-Readable Errors, and 202 + Webhooks
